This section reviews 24 existing disease modeling frameworks, plus brief notes on several more: how each one represents states, transitions, populations, networks, interventions, and time, and what we learned from it. Everything else here builds on this work by others. For help choosing a tool, see the [modeling landscape](https://starsim.org/v4/user_guide/library_landscape.html) page of the Starsim docs.

## Key takeaways

- **Few frameworks do both model structure and interventions well.** Those with the clearest model definitions ([camdl](camdl.md), [odin](odin.md), [summer2](summer2.md)) have few ready-made interventions, and those with the richest interventions ([EMOD](emod.md), [EpiHiper](epihiper.md), [Starsim](starsim.md), [Atomica](atomica.md)) have looser model definitions.
- **Transitions work best as named, declared objects.** A transition buried in code cannot easily be diagrammed, checked, or converted. Several frameworks separately arrived at splitting spontaneous transitions from those driven by contact.
- **Running one model in several paradigms has been done, but only in part.** [camdl](camdl.md), [epipack](epipack.md), and [EMULSION](emulsion.md) each run one model more than one way. The hard part is writing transmission once so that it works for mass action, contact matrices, and networks.
- **Many frameworks have found they need to tell rates, probabilities, and durations apart**, since mixing them up is an easy mistake to make.
- **Configuration files have a real tradeoff.** Models in YAML or JSON are clear about what they contain, but can be hard to write and read at length.

The [full comparison](README.md) has a table of all the frameworks and how they were chosen. Each framework has its own review, and [other frameworks](notes.md) has brief entries for the rest. The [models page](../models/index.qmd#how-the-models-were-chosen) says which frameworks have models translated into Starsim, and why the others don't.
